blocks.text: Dear Mr. Myers:

Thank you for the two mornings your people gave us. They were candid conversations, more candid than these usually are at this stage, and we are grateful for them. This letter sets out the terms on which we will conduct the search for your chief financial officer. It becomes our agreement when you sign the enclosed copy and return it to us.
The Assignment

You have asked us to find a chief financial officer for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}. We take the work on a retained basis, which means we work it exclusively and we stay with it until the seat is filled. From what your leadership described to us, the brief is a finance executive who has carried a company through a stretch of growth without letting the discipline of the close slip, who can hold a board conversation and a controller conversation on the same afternoon, and who is comfortable being the person in the room who says no. We will put that into a written position specification in the opening weeks and ask you to correct it line by line. Nothing else in this letter matters as much as getting that document right, because every candidate we approach will be approached against it, and because it is the one page on which both of us can hold the other to account.
How We Will Run the Search
We run a search in four movements, and we do not begin one before the movement in front of it is finished.

items: 1. Specification. We meet the people who will interview, including the board members, and we write the specification you sign off. We will also settle with you at that point what the role pays and what it does not, because a specification that is silent on that attracts the wrong reader.
2. Research. We map the companies where this person is most likely to be sitting today, agree that map with you, and only then work up individuals against it. Companies first, names afterwards.

3. Approach and assessment. Our consultants make the approaches themselves, and no one else does it for them. We meet the serious candidates in person and more than once, and we take references we have chosen rather than the ones a candidate offers us.

4. Slate and close. We present a short slate with a written assessment of each candidate, run the interview process around your calendar, and stay with you through the offer and the resignation that has to follow it.

blocks.text: You will hear us describe candidates by their current role rather than by name until the point they agree to meet you. That is not ceremony. The people worth having are employed and well regarded where they are, and a name that circulates is a candidate who withdraws.
Your Team

Sandra Fuentes, a Principal of this firm, leads the search and is your contact for anything touching scope, pace, or a decision that needs making. Jeffrey Patterson, our Research Consultant, builds the target list and keeps it current as the market answers back. James Grant, Senior Consultant, runs the interview calendar with your office and sits with Sandra Fuentes on the assessment work, so that two of us have met every candidate who reaches you. I hold this firm's commitment to you. If at any point the search is not going the way this letter describes, call me and say so.
Fees, Expenses, and the Start of Work

The fee for this assignment and the schedule on which it is billed are set out on the signature page of this letter, which counsel for both sides will execute with us. Expenses are billed at cost and itemized: candidate travel, our own travel to meet candidates, and background verification. We do not bill research time, telephone, courier, or administrative support, and we do not mark up an expense. Work begins {{fact:f:E-2015-001.start}}, and we would like the specification session held in that first week, while your leadership still has the conversation fresh.
Term and Termination

The engagement runs from the start date above until the position is filled, and either of us may end it earlier on thirty days' written notice. If you end it, you owe the portion of the retainer earned to that point together with expenses already incurred. If we end it, we will hand over the position specification, the research file, and an honest account of where every conversation in progress stands, so that whoever picks the search up is not starting from a blank page.
Confidentiality

We treat what we learn about {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}, its people, and its plans as confidential, and we expect the same care in the other direction for the people we bring you. Candidate materials go to the interviewing group and no further; they are not for general circulation inside the company. Neither of us will name the other in publicity about this search without written consent. For as long as this engagement is open, and for one year after it closes, we will not approach anyone employed by you on behalf of another client.
If the Placement Does Not Hold

If the executive we place leaves within the first year, for a reason other than a change you make to the role or to whom it reports, we will conduct one replacement search and you will owe only the out-of-pocket expenses of it. We ask one thing in return, which is that you tell us early when something is not working.
Limitation of Liability

We will do this work with the care and skill of a firm that has done it many times, and we do not guarantee a hire. Taken together across all claims, our liability under this letter is limited to the amounts you have actually paid us under it, and neither of us is liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss. Nothing here limits a liability that the law does not permit us to limit.
Governing Law

This letter is governed by the law of the state in which our principal office sits, and any dispute arising under it will be brought in the courts of that state. If a court sets aside any provision of this letter, the remainder stands.
If this describes our understanding, please sign both copies and return one to us. Sandra Fuentes will call your office the same day to put the specification session in the calendar.

To: Jeffrey Patterson; James Grant
Cc: James Weiss
From: Sandra Fuentes, Principal
Re: CFO search for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}} -- how we are running it

The specification will decide this search, not the length of the list, so I want the first two weeks spent earning a document that Jason Myers and the board members who sit in on the interviews would all recognize as a description of the job they are actually hiring for, and I would like the rest of this plan to bend around that. Our engagement runs from {{fact:f:E-2015-001.start}} and is scoped at about three months. Jason Myers, the chief operating officer at {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}, is our contact for everything on their side, which means scheduling, feedback on candidates, and any decision we need from them, and it also means he should not be hearing about this search from three of us in three different weeks.
What each of us is carrying

items: 1. The specification and the client relationship are mine. I will run the briefing sessions with their leadership, write the draft, and take it back for correction as many times as it needs, and nothing goes into the market until Jason Myers has signed it off.

2. Research and the target list belong to Jeffrey Patterson. I want the company map agreed with me before any individual is worked up, with the reason each company is on it written down beside it, because the reason is the part we will be asked to defend the first time a name comes back to us from their side.

3. Process and the calendar are James Grant's: interview slots, candidate travel, and the running file, and from the point the first candidates are meeting us in person he sits with me on the assessment interviews, so that two of us have met everyone who reaches the slate.
4. The engagement administration sits with James Weiss, which is the countersigned letter, the engagement code, and the billing schedule, all of which he needs closed out before the first cycle.

blocks.text: These four are not four projects running side by side. The specification disciplines the research, the research decides who we approach, and the calendar only becomes real once there is somebody to put in it. The temptation on a search with a three-month shape is to start working names in the first week so that the client can see movement, and a list built before the specification is settled has to be built a second time.

There is one thing I want tested before the specification session. The role as their leadership describes it asks for someone who has sat in the chair at a company twice their size and who will also be hands-on through a close, and at the compensation they have in mind those two things do not often live in the same person. Jeffrey Patterson, bring me whatever the map says about that. If the market disagrees with the brief, the specification session is where we have the standing to say so, and I intend to use it.
The first two weeks

Before the specification session there are three things I need, and I am asking now so that nobody is doing them the night before. Jeffrey Patterson, a first cut of the company map, deliberately broad, with the sectors you think are adjacent marked as such so that we can argue about them properly. James Grant, the calendar: I want their leadership's availability and the board members' availability held for two windows, one for the specification session and one for the first slate review. James Weiss, confirmation that the letter is back countersigned before we spend anything against the engagement.

One last thing, old ground, but it belongs at the start of a search. We describe candidates by their current role and never by name in anything that leaves this office, including notes to their side, until a candidate has agreed to meet them. That habit is the reason people who are not looking still take our calls.
CFO Search for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}

A briefing for Jason Myers and the interview group, prepared by Sandra Fuentes, with Jeffrey Patterson on research and James Grant on process. The engagement began {{fact:f:E-2015-001.start}} and is scoped to run about three months. This briefing covers the opening phase of the work: what we have done, what the market has said back to us so far, and what we would ask of you before the slate is drawn.
Where the search stands

items: The position specification is settled and signed off, and every approach we have made since has been made against it.
The company map is agreed, covering the sector itself and the two adjacent ones, with the reason each company is on it recorded.
Approaches are underway. These are conversations rather than applications; almost nobody we want is looking.
There is no slate yet, and there should not be. A slate drawn at this point would be a list of the people who answered first.

blocks.text: What the market is telling us

items: The role reads well to operators who have been through a growth stretch, and reads as a step sideways to sitting finance chiefs at much larger companies.
The board exposure written into the specification is the part that draws people in.
Two candidates asked early how decisions actually get made and who owns the annual plan. Expect that question in your interviews.
Compensation is not an obstacle so far, though we will know more once we are talking with people who would have to leave something behind.

blocks.text: How we are protecting the process

items: Candidates are described by their current role and never by name in anything that circulates, including these pages.
Jeffrey Patterson holds the target list and the reasoning behind each name, so that any candidate who reaches you can be defended.
James Grant holds the interview calendar. Windows are confirmed before a candidate is told anything about dates.
Nothing about this search is put in writing outside the engagement team and your interview group.

blocks.text: What we would ask of you

items: Two half-day windows held for the interview group, so that the slate review is not waiting on calendars once it is ready.
A view from Jason Myers on whether the board members meet finalists together or separately.
Feedback within a day of each meeting. Candidates read a long silence as a decision that has already been made.

blocks.text: Hi Jason,

The search is where it should be at this point: the specification is settled, the company map is agreed, and we are into the approaches. I am opening this thread so that the running record of the {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}} search sits in one place instead of scattered across separate notes, and I have copied Jeffrey Patterson and James Grant so that nothing waits on my being at my desk. Anything you send back on this thread reaches all three of us, which is the point of it.

There are a couple of things we could use from your side. If your office can hold two half-days for the interview group over the next few weeks, we can build the slate review around them instead of chasing calendars once it is ready. The other is one line in the specification that is still doing more work than it should, the part about ownership of the annual plan, and I would like ten minutes on the phone with you to settle whether that sits with the new chief financial officer or stays where it is today. Whichever way it lands, we want it settled before candidates are sitting in front of you, because it is the first thing a serious finance person asks about.

I have attached the plan we set at kickoff so you can see the sequence we are working to. The first written progress note will reach you in a couple of weeks, and sooner than that if anything changes you would want to know about.
Best regards
Working Session -- CFO Search for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}

The session was called to review the working list before the slate is drawn, and it reached one decision that changes the sequence: the second research pass will be widened to two adjacent sectors before any name goes in front of the client, which moves the slate review back by about a week. These minutes record who attended, what was discussed in the order it came up, what was decided, and who owns each next step.
Present

items: Sandra Fuentes, Principal, Northgate Talent Partners
Jeffrey Patterson, Research Consultant, Northgate Talent Partners
James Grant, Senior Consultant, Northgate Talent Partners (minutes)
Jason Myers, Chief Operating Officer, {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}

blocks.text: The working list

Jeffrey Patterson took the room through the working list, describing each candidate by current role and by the kind of company rather than by name, as we do until a candidate has agreed to meet the client. The list falls into three groups: sitting finance chiefs at companies of roughly the client's size, deputies at larger companies who would be stepping up into the seat, and a small number of operators who have held the seat before and since moved into something broader. He was direct that the second group is where the interest is strongest and also where the uncertainty is, since a first-time chief financial officer is a judgment call that references can only partly settle.
The reservation put on the record

Jason Myers accepted the shape of the list and then raised, twice and in different words, a concern that the candidates described to him had all come out of the same sector, and that a finance chief who has only ever worked in one industry would arrive with a narrower set of instincts than the role will need over the next several years. Sandra Fuentes took the point rather than argue it, and asked Jim to sit with Jeffrey Patterson on the second research pass so that the two of them widen the map together and do not end up reading the same list differently. Jason Myers also said, in passing and without pressing it, that the date matters less to him than the quality of the list, and the remark is recorded here because it should govern the pace from this point on.
Interview logistics

James Grant reported that the client's office has held two half-day windows for the interview group and that the board members' availability, not the executives', is the binding constraint on both. Sandra Fuentes asked that no candidate be told a date until both windows are confirmed in writing, on the grounds that a date offered and then withdrawn costs us more with a candidate than a delay does. Jason Myers undertook to confirm the board side through his own office.
Actions

rows: Widen the research map into the two adjacent sectors and re-cut the working list
Sit with research on the second pass, and hold candidate dates until both interview windows are confirmed in writing
Confirm both interview windows, including the board members' availability
Redraft the candidate summary format so each candidate is described by role and by the evidence behind the judgment

blocks.text: The next session will take the re-cut list in the same order these minutes follow, and it will not be scheduled until the widened map is in hand.
Status Report: CFO Search for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}

Prepared for the leadership group at {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}} by Sandra Fuentes, Principal. The search is on track, and the matter that should hold your attention is not the pace but the shape of the list: we have widened the research into two adjacent sectors, which sets us back the better part of a week and which we think is plainly the right call, and it means the slate you see will be broader than the one described at the briefing. The rest of this report sits behind that.
Where the search stands

We are at roughly the midpoint. The position specification has not moved since it was signed off, which is worth saying, because a specification that keeps changing under a search is the usual reason one runs long. The company map is complete and has now been extended past the original sector. Approaches are well advanced: first conversations have happened with the great majority of the working list, and second conversations are underway with the people who are serious about it. James Grant and I have between us met every candidate likely to reach the slate, in person and more than once, which is the standard we hold to before a name is put in front of a client.

Two things the approaches have surfaced are worth passing on now, because they will show up in your interviews. The role reads as a genuine step up to deputies at larger companies, and it reads as a lateral move to sitting finance chiefs well above your size, which is why the second of those groups has produced fewer real conversations than the map suggested it would. And the question that comes back most often is not about the numbers at all; it is about who owns the annual plan and how much room the seat has to change it. A consistent answer to that from everyone who interviews will do more for this search than anything we write down.
What has closed out in this period
Several pieces of work finished in this period, and I set them down so that your team can see where the ground is now firm.

items: 1. The position specification was signed off and circulated to the interview group, and every approach we have made since has been made against it.
2. Jeffrey Patterson completed the company map and then extended it, on our own initiative, into the two adjacent sectors raised at the working session.
3. First approaches are complete across the original sector, and second conversations are underway with the candidates who have real interest in the role.

4. James Grant has the interview architecture in place: two half-day windows held with your office, the board members' availability confirmed, and an agreed written format for the candidate summaries that will come to you with the slate.
5. Reference work has started early on the strongest two candidates, using references we have chosen ourselves rather than the ones we were offered.

blocks.text: The period ahead

The next stretch does three things. Jeffrey Patterson re-cuts the working list against the widened map, and that piece sets the pace for everything after it. We then run the assessment interviews to a close and finish the reference work, writing each candidate up in the format James Grant agreed with your office. After that we present the slate in a session rather than by email, because the discussion in the room is what makes the written summaries useful, and we would want your interview group there for it. No candidate will be given a date until both interview windows are confirmed.
What could still go wrong
Three risks are worth your attention, and none of them needs a decision from you today.

items: 1. The calendar. The board members' availability, not your executives', is the binding constraint on the interview process, and a week that slips there is a week in which a candidate being courted somewhere else makes a different decision.

2. The step-up question. A good part of the strength on this list sits with deputies at larger companies who would be moving into the seat for the first time. They are the more interesting candidates and they carry the greater uncertainty, so each summary will set out exactly what the evidence for the judgment is and where that evidence runs out.

3. Discretion. Everyone on this list is employed and well regarded where they are. We describe candidates to you by their current role until they have agreed to meet, and we would ask that the summaries stay inside the interview group. It takes very little for someone who was not looking in the first place to decide the risk is not worth it.

blocks.text: What we need from you

Feedback speed after the interviews, more than anything else. If each interviewer can get us a view within a day of meeting a candidate, we can hold a process together; at a week, candidates start reading the silence, and the ones with options act on what they read. I will call your office next week to walk you through the re-cut list before any of it is written down.
